summary: Budget week: Ottawa tables its budget Thursday after weak growth numbers and a rate hike, while Carney says a Sunday call with Trump moved trade talks forward.
body: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne tables the federal budget on Thursday, November 5 (yesterday's brief wrongly called it Wednesday) [^1]. It is titled "Masters of Our Destiny" and framed around Canada's sovereignty, but no measures have been announced [^2]. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre wants federal diesel taxes paused until Canada Day and spending cut [^3]. Since winning three byelections in April, the Liberals hold a majority, so the budget is expected to pass [^7].

It arrives in a weak economy. Statistics Canada says the economy did not grow in August, the second flat month in a row, and an early estimate shows a small drop in September [^4]. Auto plant shutdowns and the August breakdown of trade talks, which brought new tariffs on both sides, are among the reasons [^4]. The Bank of Canada still raised its key rate to 2.5% on Oct. 28, its first hike in over three years, because of inflation risks [^4]. Higher rates make borrowing for cars, homes and student lines of credit more expensive.

On trade, Prime Minister Mark Carney called his Sunday talk with President Trump a "good conversation" and said teams will work "in the coming weeks" toward a deal [^5][^6]. No terms have been announced, and US tariffs of 50% still cover about $20 billion of Canadian goods [^6]. In Toronto, the province finished removing 1.2 km of bike lanes on Bloor Street West and plans more on Bloor, University and Yonge [^8]. My read: Thursday's budget will show how much Ottawa is willing to borrow to cushion the trade war.
differences: Carney says the operating budget will balance by 2027-28; the Parliamentary Budget Officer expects that to slip a year [^1]. On trade, McGill's Daniel Béland says the White House sees political risk in the dispute, while U of T historian Robert Bothwell calls the thaw "5 minutes of variable sunshine" [^6]. Economists split on whether weak growth means the Bank of Canada will pause in December [^4].
